General Strike Disrupts Cambodian Economy as Workers Demand Higher Wages

PHNOM PENH, June 28—A general strike involving workers from multiple sectors brought economic activity across Cambodia to a near standstill on Friday, as tens of thousands of employees walked off the job demanding higher wages and improved working conditions.

Public transportation in the capital ground to a halt early in the morning, with city buses and many taxi services suspended. The strike spread swiftly to manufacturing hubs in Kandal, Kampong Speu, and Svay Rieng provinces, where garment and electronics factories remained shuttered throughout the day.

According to the Cambodian Confederation of Trade Unions, more than 120,000 workers participated in the action nationwide. “We are united in our call for a living wage,” said union leader Sokha Nhem, addressing a crowd outside the Ministry of Labor. “Our families cannot survive on current salaries as the cost of living keeps rising.”

Banks, schools, and many public offices reported reduced operations, while several major markets in Phnom Penh and Siem Reap closed their doors. The Cambodian Association of Small Businesses estimated that daily commercial losses could exceed $15 million if the stoppage continues.

“We are extremely concerned about the impact on exports,” said Chenda Sary, spokesperson for the Cambodia Exporters Federation. “Our members report shipments delayed at ports and orders put on hold. This disrupts supply chains and could threaten Cambodia’s reputation as a reliable trade partner.”

Government officials urged calm and called for dialogue. “We respect the right to peaceful protest, but urge all parties to return to the negotiating table,” Labor Ministry spokesman Khun Dara told reporters. “Uninterrupted economic activity is vital for national development and stability.”

Analysts noted that the strike comes amid mounting inflation and ongoing debates over minimum wage reform. “This reflects deep frustration among workers, especially after a year of rising food and fuel prices,” said Piseth Chan, an economist at the Royal Institute of Cambodia.

As of late Friday, union leaders indicated the strike would continue until government and employer representatives agreed to substantive talks on wage increases and workplace protections. Police reported isolated roadblocks but no major incidents.
